## Paper

Artificial Intelligence and Auction Design

## World

auction_house

## Institution

First-price and second-price auction formats under learning agents.

## Agent type

Q-learning or algorithmic bidders.

## Theoretical benchmark

Auction format changes learned bidding, bid shading, revenue, and efficiency.

## Learning setup

Repeated auctions where agents learn bids from private-value observations.

## Metrics

Revenue, underbidding/bid shading, efficiency, surplus, regret, learned bid curves.

## Main result

First-price auctions with no additional feedback lead to tacit-collusive outcomes (bids lower than values), while second-price auctions do not. Providing information about the lowest bid to win increases competitiveness of first-price auctions.

## What they prove

The paper provides model-specific theoretical and computational evidence about how auction format and feedback affect learned bidding behavior. Treat its first-price/second-price contrast as a benchmark for diagnostics, not as a universal guarantee for all learned auction settings.

## What they only simulate

Learned bid paths, coordination patterns, feedback variants, reserve effects, and bidder-count variants in the paper's configured auction-learning settings.

## What they do NOT test

This repo's fixed world/mind/institution ladder, deep-RL/MARL comparisons across non-auction worlds, and the exact bid-grid/training protocol used here.

## What we need to reproduce

Compare first-price bid shading and second-price truthfulness-like behavior using learned bid curves and regret.

## How our project differs

The paper studies AI and auction design. This repo implements a controlled Auction House world and validates mechanics before cross-mind passes.

## Implementation obligations

First-price payment; second-price payment; bid-shading benchmark; learned bid-curve output; format-by-format summary table.

## Metrics to compare in our repo

Auction House first_price and second_price learned bid curves; outputs/auction_house_full.

## Failure modes to audit

No learned bid-curve inspection; using revenue alone to rank formats; no reserve/no-sale semantics; no benchmark-case tests.

## Project code comparison

Compare Artificial Intelligence and Auction Design to Auction House Q-learning full outputs. The repo has the right diagnostics for bidder behavior, but cross-mind auction claims remain pending until full ladder runs are interpreted.

We find that first-price auctions with no additional feedback lead to tacit-collusive outcomes (bids lower than values), while second-price auctions do not. We show that the difference is driven by the incentive in first-price auctions to outbid opponents by just one bid increment.
